Mr. J. B. McGeachy, until recently of the Globe and Mail. I do not think we can call Mr. McGeachy a leftist.
There are many of us who could.

If that is the case I think we had better skip that matter, because we cannot find any common ground.
I rise at this time particularly to support my colleague the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond in expressing quite candidly what I think is the opinion of British Columbia. During the Easter recess we had the largest and most enthusiastic Liberal convention that has ever been held in the history of the province, at which people from all over the province of British Columbia devised a new platform for the party. One of the points which was passed by an overwhelming majority was that there should be in Canada a new name for the controlling body of radio and television in this country. I forget exactly what they called it, but the substance of the recommendation was that instead of having a board of governors in charge and control over both the C.B.C. and the private stations, we should have a new independent tribunal over both of them.
At this point may I say that while I am personally in favour of it and shall certainly support it, as I supported it in this house some three years ago, I do not believe there was in that proposal as much substance as there is in the proposal made by my colleague the hon. member of Burnaby-Richmond. In my opinion it will not make very much difference what may be the name of the body that controls radio and television in Canada, because if they took effective control of radio and television in Canada all they would do would be to put in my good friend Mr. Davidson Dunton as chairman of the new body. They could not find a better man in Canada. He is by far the most competent radio and television man there is in Canada. Hence all that it would do would be to give a new title to an old job. But I think it would perhaps take the C.B.C. out of the false position in which it is so often accused of being, namely of being both judge, jury and policeman and all the rest of it. It would take it out of that false position.

I happen to be a little luckier than my hon. friend. I hear some of the comments by C.B.C. commentators on the other side. I heard a very good commentary by Mr. Wilson Woodside, who not so many months ago ran as the Conservative candidate for Trinity and is a man who could not by any stretch of the imagination be called a leftist. Then I often hear, and with great pleasure,
But as to the question of competition in Vancouver and in British Columbia generally, I am personally quite convinced that at least 95 per cent or I suppose I could go even higher than that and say well over 95 per cent-of the people of Vancouver certainly cannot see any sense in our being forced to choose between listening to or viewing a C.B.C. television station and the competing

Supply-C.B.C.
private stations in the United States. We believe in competition. We believe in plenty of competition. The only thing in which I differ with my hon. friend the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond is this. He wants to put up some kind of iron curtain around the borders of Burnaby. I do not think that would be quite practical.
I think perhaps this is what differentiates me from some of my friends immediately opposite. Sometimes I have noted in them what I would call a hostility to private enterprise as such. Some of my hon. friends even seem hostile to the idea of anybody starting a private television station and making money. For what it is worth I say this. If 50 people construct private stations and make money, that suits me fine. I think we can do with one or two of them in and around Vancouver, and all to the good. My policy is to let anybody do anything in the way of private business as long as he is not doing anything that hurts anybody else.
That brings me to an extremely important point. I will frankly confess that if anybody could show me that it was impossible to licence these competitive outlets and still maintain the C.B.C. in the prosperous and sound condition in which it is from coast to coast, I myself would be against any change. Let me make this absolutely clear, Mr. Chairman. I regard the C.B.C. as perhaps the greatest single agency which has yet been built up in this country for the creation of national unity and harmony in this Dominion of Canada. Whatever else we have or do not have, let us never forget the great debt we owe to the C.B.C. It has done a great service to the people of Canada, and it is doing a great service right now.
It is not perfect. I have never met any perfect people. I have never known of any perfect political parties. I have never seen any perfect newspapers. I do not know of any perfect institution anywhere. The C.B.C. is not perfect. I do not expect it to adopt all my ideas or to agree with my ideas which are fairly lowbrow in some respects. For instance, every night is Wednesday as far as the C.B.C. are concerned. They have too much Tschaikovsky and not enough cowboy music, especially in the morning; and I cannot "go" Tschaikovsky before 10 a.m.
I do not expect everybody to agree with me. By and large I think the C.B.C. is doing a wonderful job. Whatever else we do or do not do, I think every intelligent and patriotic person in Canada should make absolutely certain that we keep the C.B.C. in operation, and that we put up whatever amount of money is necessary for that purpose from time to time. While I for one
[Mr. Philpottl
would not dream of trying to anticipate anything the Fowler commission might recommend, I certainly have no compunction in expressing my own personal hopes. Those hopes include the one that, whatever is recommended, the C.B.C. will be kept in flourishing condition; that it will be given the means to do its own job; that it will have taken away from it some of the tasks which it ought never to have been given in the first place and which put it in a false light with regard to some of its own competitors.
Regardless of how the money is raised to finance the operations of the C.B.C., it seems to me that if the C.B.C. can continue to do as good a job for the people of Canada as it has done in the past, it could come before the parliament of Canada every year with its budget and ask for whatever amount of money it needed to do a good job and be reasonably sure of getting it from this house and from the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, there is one thing of which we can be certain when we discuss the estimates of the C.B.C. There is always a great variety of opinion. Certainly this afternoon, in the speakers who have taken part thus far, we have seen the same situation repeat itself. I think it was in the issue of April 2, 1955, that Maclean's magazine presented an extremely interesting article under the heading, "Everybody Throws Rocks at Davey". In that article they were referring to the chairman of the board. A few rocks have been thrown this afternoon and also a few bouquets. I am not going to decide just how the score stands at the moment.
However, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that by the very nature of things there is bound to be long and bitter discussion on a subject of this kind, where you have a broadcasting agency growing larger and larger and more powerful and more powerful under the control of the state. It has been said by some speakers here this afternoon that we have a public utility in the C.B.C., providing a public service. In some respects that is quite true. In this instance, however, we have a public utility, we have a crown corporation dabbling in the very controversial arena of ideas. There are as many ideas or different opinions as there are people in this world. When the broadcasting media are under the control of the state, as they are at the present time, we are bound to have great difference of opinion and rather acrimonious debate.
Actually it is a good thing that we have this opportunity of discussing the C.B.C. estimates at least once a year. Even from the comments that have been made already it is

obvious that there is a need, for changes in our broadcasting policy, and that there is need for very careful criticism and analysis. I think that has been recognized in the appointment of the Fowler commission which, very shortly, will be bringing in a comprehensive report on the state of broadcasting in this country. Upon that report members of this house will be able to base a more or less comprehensive judgment as to what shall be done in the future.
I listened to the statement of the Minister of National Revenue yesterday and today in reporting to the house on the operations of the C.B.C. As he gave us his statement the thought occurred to me that the C.B.C. has a lion by the tail in broadcasting matters in Canada, particularly since the advent of television. This applies particularly to the rapidly rising costs of providing an adequate television service. The minister's report suggested that we have increased coverage; we have increased programming, and what is perhaps most important, we have increased costs. Everything in the field of broadcasting in the last four years has been getting bigger and "better"-I will put that last word in inverted commas in relation to the C.B.C. activities. I am quite willing to agree that the level of C.B.C. programming has improved in the T.V. medium, but that is to be expected when we recall the tremendous amounts of money that are being devoted to this new mass medium of communication.
However, Canada is rich in talent. There is no reason at all why Canada should not be in a position to provide programs that are equal to the best that can be provided by broadcasting activities in any other country. It is not because the C.B.C. is largely a state operation that we have excellent programs. Under any conditions of broadcasting we would have this same talent available. It could be argued, of course, that the state monopoly of broadcasting, rigid state control, might serve to inhibit creativity rather than stimulate it. Other major countries which are extensively engaged in telecasting at the present time also present worth-while programs.
I am glad to see that the C.B.C. is going to extend its activities so far as the international exchange of worth-while programs is concerned. I suppose the country which has the greatest output of high calibre programs for various reasons is our neighbour to the south, the United States. They have the resources, the talent and the manpower. They also have the greatest degree of freedom in broadcasting activities. I have before me a report that I took out of a U.S.S.R. picture magazine for May, 1956. It reports extensively on the aims and tasks of broadcasting in the U.S.S.R. There they have a
Supply-C.B.C.
state-controlled broadcasting service, of course, and the paragraph which sums up their objectives says something to this effect: The Soviet people do not regard the radio solely as a means of getting news or entertainment. They regard it as a means of broadening their store of knowledge and of keeping in contact with all the developments in world culture. It is in line with this approach that radio programs and television programs are worked out. They go on to outline the kind of programs they are doing in that country.
It is quite true that there are various ways of handling this important medium of communication in Canada which, in a relatively short time, has made a fair degree of progress. But I still say it is possible to argue that the rigid control in this country has inhibited rather than encouraged creativity. The matter of programming seems to be the main reason for the rapid rise in the cost of Canadian telecasting. I should like to raise a query as to whether, in order to carry out the announced functions of C.B.C., it is advisable for us to concentrate so extensively on the provision of light entertainment. There are several fairly costly programs of this kind that are promoted by the C.B.C. Most of them are imitations of similar United States variety shows, and are justified as talent producers. Unfortunately, as the minister mentioned last night, as soon as the artists achieve any degree of fame on the network in Canada there is a tendency for the talent to be lured across the border, where the opportunities are wider and the financial inducements greater.
The minister explained that phenomenon as an indication that Canada has reached maturity in the talent field. It is a rather left-handed compliment to Canada that our entertainers are invited across to wider fields in the United States talent market. That, of course, is one explanation; but it is a phenomenon that has unfortunately been occurring for years, that Canada's outstanding talent, not only in the entertainment field but also in other professional fields has been going to the United States. It is something that has not been in the best interests of the country.
I think there is another explanation that might be given, and that is that there is under the present semi-monopolistic position of broadcasting under the control of the C.B.C., no other outlet for entertainment talent in Canada. If a professional entertainer does not find favour with the C.B.C. he has no other place to turn in Canada, and therefore must find his way across the border.
This situation arises particularly because of the C.B.C. monopely of network facilities.

Supply-C.B.C.
The criticism is made from time to time that the private broadcasters have not encouraged Canadian talent to the same extent as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Well, that is quite understandable when we realize that in order to provide programs of the same high calibre it would be necessary for the private operator, under existing regulations, to carry the full burden of the expense on his own financial resources, whereas the C.B.C. with its broad national network resources can pool the expenses right across the network, as well as being subsidized by the public treasury. If the private stations had the same privilege of pooling expenses there is no doubt they could make a broader and wider contribution to the improvement of programming in both the radio and television fields.
The basic function of the C.B.C., the original purpose in establishing a national service, was to knit Canada together as a closer national unit. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the hon. member for Vancouver South, said that the greatest contribution in this regard has been made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I was glad to hear him make that confession, because hitherto I had always heard it was the Liberal party that had made the greatest contribution in that regard. I will say that the C.B.C. has done an outstanding job in establishing a national point of view-
Different fields, entirely.

-in helping to knit this diverse geographic expanse together, and that was one of the original basic purposes in establishing a national Canadian broadcasting system. Second, there was the important function of bringing a Canadian content, in the first instance, to our radio programs and now to our television programs. These same functions still remain, and it is in these areas that C.B.C. can serve its most useful purpose. But here again I should like to suggest that as changes have taken place in broadcasting in Canada, the private operators have moved into this area to a much greater extent than was originally expected. For example, we have now some 150 private stations helping to weld Canada together culturally as compared with some 30 C.B.C. radio stations-I am not sure of the exact number-and even in the television field there are more private outlets today than there are C.B.C. outlets.
Notwithstanding the limited resources of the private broadcasters, that have risen from the circumstances I outlined a few moments ago. They have been doing some quite worthwhile programming. Therefore, while the C.B.C. has for its two basic functions the matter of national unity and the provision of
TMr. Dinsdale.]
Canadian content, I think their job today has been lessened considerably by the increase of influence and responsibility of the private broadcasters since the advent of national broadcasting back in 1932.
Perhaps we would be able to deal with this problem of rapidly accumulating costs that has been mentioned by the minister as the bugbear of telecasting in Canada if we used to a greater extent than we are using at the present time the broadcast facilities that are so readily available through the operations of the private stations. Certainly the C.B.C. expenses could be reduced considerably by this method.
I notice that a few days ago-I think it was mentioned in this house-that an experiment was going to be undertaken to make it possible for private operators to carry on a limited network operation. I think that is a step in the right direction, because there is no reason at all why the private stations should be restricted to the local spheres of operation, as they have in the past, and not given wider access to the national radio or television listening audiences. Certainly, it would provide a more representative program and better cultural coverage of the nation if we could get more programs from the local community level than we do at the present time. Under the present set-up a good many of our programs tend to originate in the larger urban centres, which might not necessarily be truly representative of Canadian grass roots culture.
I agree with the minister that we should leave a comprehensive discussion of broadcasting until such time as we have the Fowler report before us, but I do want to mention this one further matter before I resume my seat, and that is the question of the regulation of broadcasting in Canada. This group has never disagreed with the principle that regulation of broadcasting is needed. Obviously, in a communication media so important and so influential as broadcasting, regulations are needed and are carried out in all countries at the present time. But there does seem to be a growing demand for some independence of regulation in Canada.
I raised this issue at the present time because of something that occurred in the Manitoba legislature last March. In view of the fact that I am a member from Manitoba I think it is important that the Manitoba point of view be placed on the record. Certainly we would avoid a lot of the bitterness, a lot of the misunderstanding that arises from time to time in discussions on the C.B.C. if we could remove the suspicion that there was too close a link-up between regulation and the government, for example.

Earlier in the debate we had a suggestion from the hon. member for Hamilton South that the C.B.C. errs too far in favouring the opposition, and he seemed to be bringing forth the thesis that unless the C.B.C. is speaking on behalf of the government it is not performing its function adequately. That seemed to be the implication of his statement.
No.
Well, he was criticizing the C.B.C. because it seemed to favour the opposition point of view in a particular debate that took place in this house.

Surely the hon. member realizes that the whole point made by the hon. member for Hamilton South was the allegation, which he backed up by some evidence, that during a certain debate in this house the news reports were slanted in favour of the opposition. He was not pleading for propaganda; he was pleading against slanted news reports.

That was just his opinion. Then he went on to say further the only way that could be overcome would be by having C.B.C. reporters in the gallery, which suggested that they might be more amenable to the government point of view. That was the implication behind his presentation, as I took it. Rather than move in this direction I think it is imperative that we set up some sort of independent regulatory body to avoid any suspicion of that sort of close tie-up between the government and its broadcasting agency, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I have in my hand a long statement that was made in the Manitoba legislature last march by a Liberal member who took just the opposite point of view. If time afforded I would read it. This takes an opposite point of view from that of the hon. member for Hamilton South, and claims that the C.B.C. is always pro-government and does not allow a fair airing of the other side of the question. We have two sides of the coin, one presented by a Liberal member in this house and one presented by a Liberal member in the Manitoba legislature. Certainly we should take steps just as quickly as possible to avoid any allegations and misunderstandings of that kind.
A monopoly of any kind comes under suspicion and, of course, a state monopoly comes under even more suspicion because it combines not only economic power but political power as well. The sooner we rid the C.B.C. of any shadow of doubt concerning the combination of political and economic power the sooner we will rid ourselves of at 67509-423
Supply-C.B.C.
least some of this rock throwing that has been taking place in the past few years.
Professor Marcus Long was mentioned in the discussion today. I think he came to the nub of the matter in a statement made in Vancouver recently, when he said:
I am opposed to any more government control than is necessary . . . If it is necessary to err between control and freedom it is better to err on the side of freedom. That is, increase the number of private stations rather than increase government monopoly and control.
On the subject of regulation, Mr. Chairman, this is what the Manitoba legislature had to say. A resolution was passed and approved in March, 1956, by a vote of 46 to 5, which is one of the largest majorities which has been given any resolution in the Manitoba legislature within recent days. The resolution was phrased in these terms:
Whereas, Manitoba citizens have a wide choice of radio stations;
And whereas, there has been a demand for the establishment of more than one local television station;
And whereas, due to Manitoba's geographic position, a great number of our citizens have but one choice of a television station;
And whereas, it is desirable that Manitoba citizens have a wider selection of television stations;
Therefore be it resolved that this house go on record as favouring competition in the television broadcasting field in the greater Winnipeg area;
And be it further resolved that the federal government be urged to encourage the establishment of television stations in other parts of the province of Manitoba.
Then an amendment was moved which was passed with an unprecedented majority of 47 to 5. The amendment reads:
Be it still further resolved that the federal government be urged to set up and establish an independent board of regulation for Canadian broadcasting.
We are dealing with a very controversial and complex field, and nothing I can say at this time will throw any further light on the matter. I think it would be in the interests of the best functioning of the C.B.C. if we move toward a more representative position for private broadcasters in this important field, and further if just as soon as possible we establish an independent regulatory body that would remove any shadow of suspicion of political interference in the important function of broadcasting.

Mr. Chairman, I was extremely surprised, as I am sure all hon. members of the house must have been, to hear the hon. member for Hamilton South this afternoon make a charge-which was very vigorously applauded by the many Liberal members in the house at the time-that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Canadian Press and the British United Press, the two news services which supply the Canadian

Supply-C.B.C.
Broadcasting Corporation with its news, and the press gallery in general are guilty of slanting the news.
I have been a member of this parliament for six years -
Too long.

-and during that time I have become convinced that the C.B.C., the Canadian Press, the British United Press and the press gallery generally report the news both fairly and objectively. From time to time each hon. member, of course, feels that certain speeches did not receive the reporting which they merited. On the other hand, if each one of us is honest he will admit that at times we are very pleasantly surprised by the reporting we do receive, and often we must admit to ourselves that our speeches appear better when we read them in the paper than they perhaps sounded or than we ourselves thought they were.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Speak for yourself, George.
Of course I know that the Minister of Finance always thinks his speeches are masterpieces, but I am just an ordinary man and I know I make some which I must admit are only fair.
So do the rest of us.

I think a vast majority of the hon. members in this house will agree that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Canadian Press, the British United Press and the press gallery generally call them as they see them, and that they are very fair indeed. In sports, Mr. Chairman, one learns to take the referee's decision without whining.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: You have not learned that yet.

Oh, yes, I have. That is one thing I have learned. I have never complained about a referee's decision in my whole life, and I'll bet you have, if you ever did happen to participate in sports, which I doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: You complained about 24 of the Speaker's rulings in one month.
Mr. Chairman, before the growling started across the line-and it is nice to hear the hon. members on the other side start squealing, because it shows we are sticking them where it hurts-*
Oh, don't be like your leader.

The hon. member for Hamilton South and the many Liberal members in the house at the time who applauded him so vigorously whined this afternoon when they

claimed that the reports given by the C.B.C., which were given to the C.B.C. by the Canadian Press and British United Press concerning the pipe-line debate, were not flattering to the Liberal party.
They were lies.

Practically every newspaper of every political stripe in this country from coast to coast vigorously criticized the Liberal party's policy and conduct in that pipe-line debate. To single out the C.B.S.'s reports in this instance is, I believe, whining on a very large scale. From what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Hamilton South I can only conclude that he and the Liberal members who applauded him so enthusiastically would like to see the proceedings of parliament reported-
Correctly.

by government-selected C.B.C. parliamentary observers over whom the government could exert complete control. Then the people of Canada would receive only the government's version of what transpired in this house.
They would receive a true report.
Verbatim.

That, Mr. Chairman, would be an important step forward in the creation of the dictatorship which this government's conduct in the pipe-line debate made very clear this government is determined to achieve. I think it was interesting and rather shocking to hear what we have felt has been going on for some time so clearly expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Hamilton South and so loudly applauded by Liberal members who were obviously behind him 100 per cent in everything he said.

Mr. Chairman, late last evening and this afternoon we have been listening to members of the Conservative, C.C.F. and Liberal parties express their views with respect to the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. With much of what has been said I certainly can agree. We agree that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has a very important role to play in the development of the cultural life of Canada. We recognize that many of the issues which are before the corporation at this time, particularly in connection with finance and its relations with the independent broadcasting business in Canada, are matters which deserve our consideration and ought to be resolved satisfactorily as soon as possible.

There are many matters on which we as reasonable men can differ, and in this case the political angle is involved; but I think we will all agree that radio and television, by reason of their impact on commerce, and their daily place in education and entertainment, exercise a tremendous influence upon the public's interpretation of political and social events. For these reasons the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the radio and television industry have a tremendous influence upon our national life. They constitute the most powerful mass medium of communication of our time. In the world of scientific and sociological changes there are bound to be many sensitive problems which have to be tackled, some of which are very controversial. Judging from the speeches which have been made by various hon. members, we are faced with a wide difference of opinion.
In discussing the estimates of the C.B.C. we have an opportunity to examine the entire management picture, and to stress the need of economy. I think one important matter which deserves consideration at this time is the relationship existing between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the independent broadcasting industry. The annual report of the C.B.C. does not refer at any great length to this, but it is an extremely significant matter. We of the Social Credit group believe that it is an important question which involves us very directly. After all, the reason we are here is to see that there is a proper balance between the various industries of Canada, particularly in this field.
Last year we welcomed the suggestion that a royal commission be set up and we are looking forward to receiving the report of the commission. The order in council setting up the commission stated specifically that it should study the licensing and control of private television and sound broadcasting stations in the public interest. We of the Social Credit group approach this entire problem from the standpoint that there ought to be fair treatment for all and special privilege for none. We approach it from the position that there ought to be full co-operation, that there ought to be freedom, and that in this field as in all others there should be righteous competition which would be good for both parties.
Therefore we are opposed to seeing this field ruled or regulated by the excessive power of a government monopoly, which we maintain in this case is the C.B.C., just as we are opposed to private monopoly and excessive power for private money interests which may be interested in this particular field. In either case it is the public who 67509-423i
Supply-C.B.C.
are the losers. There seems to be a trend toward power grabbing and we submit that as members of parliament this should receive our thoughtful consideration.
The Fowler commission has been sitting, and the minister indicated last evening that many submissions had been made. I do not intend to touch upon these, as I think it would be improper to do so. It was my pleasure last year to be a member of the parliamentary committee which studied the affairs of the C.B.C. That committee had many issues before it, many of which also were brought before the royal commission.
Many people have been expressing the fear of abuse and injustice resulting from excess power in the hands of the C.B.C. They claim that this excessive power to regulate the activities of competitors may lend itself *at some future date to abuse. The C.B.C., being directly under government control, the inference has been that either this administration or possibly some future administration may abuse that power and become less dedicated to the principle of impartiality. Clearly we do not want anything like that to happen in Canada. However, I think I am correct when I say that abuse is taking place and has taken place.
Because of the actions of the C.B.C. the people of the province of Alberta have experienced injustice and humiliation and I would say insult. A serious situation has been created. It is encouraging and commendable to know that there are newspapers in this country prepared to report some of these startling facts. I hold in my hand a clipping from the King's County Record of June 28, 1956.
C.B.C. Controls Thought
The Fowler commission on broadcasting can surely have no more doubts about C.B.C.'s control of thought in this country- When one of the commissioners stated that the C.B.C. does not "vet" scripts on private stations, these facts came to light.
A group of Alberta stations was broadcasting a series of programs in which Alberta government leaders reported their activities to the people. C.B.C.'s Mr. George Young, who is in charge of broadcast regulations, immediately sent a curt telegram demanding that copies of the speeches be mailed to him at once so that C.B.C. could study the matter.
If C.B.C. does not "vet" such scripts, why ask for them? What do they do with them? Paper the walls of Jarvis street studios, perhaps?
As a result of harrassing these three stations the broadcast was dropped. Consequently the people of Alberta were denied a service and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as an agency of government, was able, by the threat of enforcement of regulations, to stop the flow of opinions contrary to their party's interests.
This is political interference of the worst kind. It is even worse than line by line censorship. It is thought control by threat.
The royal commission on broadcasting must have access to the files of Mr. Young, who enforces

Supply-C.B.C.
C.B.C. regulations. A study of those files would give an indication of the extent to which the C.B.C. has entered into the political arena with its regulatory powers. Will such a study be made? It should be. and without loss of time.
I am satisfied that, from the circumstances of this case I have reported to you, which took place in Alberta, it is clear that the C.B.C. and the federal government, which after all has guardianship responsibilities over the C.B.C., have offended and done injury to the purpose of the act itself. In any event, the C.B.C.'s action and the manner in which it handled this case without tact-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he say when that alleged program was on the air?
This particular incident took place some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: What year?
I believe it took place in 1951 or 1952.
Oh; ancient history.
It is not ancient history at all. These are facts that have not been disclosed to the people, and that is my reason for bringing the matter to the attention of the house.
Would the hon. member permit a question? He was a member of the radio committee. Why did he not bring it up before that committee?
When the hon. member spoke a few moments ago I listened very intently to him. If he has any further comments to make, I am sure the house would be delighted to hear him afterward.
It is a plain question. Why did not the hon. member bring up this matter in the radio committee, when he could have had Mr. George Young and all the other gentlemen and the documents?

Business of the House be imposed on the people of Canada. In my view the taxes which the people of this country are carrying at the present time are intolerable. It is quite obvious and clear that there is a need for economizing. In my opinion the C.B.C. deserves a sympathetic approach with respect to the financial difficulties they have at this time; but if they are to get that approach from the public, I think they ought to rid themselves of the idea that they do not have to reform themselves.

Question No. 555*-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough):
1.	Are there any public relations officers in the Department of National Defence?
2.	If so, how many in each branch of the service?
3.	What duties do they perform?
4.	If separation allowance, assigned pay, etc., is discontinued to the wife of a serviceman, do these officers contact the family and give reasons for discontinuance of same?
If not, does anyone in the department inform the wife or family that allowance is discontinued, and give reasons for such action?
6. How is the wife or family so informed?
Answer by. Mr. Hellyer, Parliamentary Assistant, for the Minister of National Defence:
1.	Yes.
2.	Navy, 15; army, 22; air force, 17.
3.	The main duties of public relations
officers are:	(a) to facilitate a flow of
Question
unclassified news about the armed forces to the Canadian public; (b) to give advice and information at appropriate levels in their respective services about the various aspects of a suitable over-all public relations program; (c) to advise upon and implement as appropriate-particularly at overseas establishments-a program designed to foster and maintain friendly relationships between service establishments and adjacent civilian communities.
